source.title: Mixture-of-Modules: Reinventing Transformers as Dynamic Assemblies of Modules
source.authors: Zhuo-Cheng Gong; Ang Lv; Jian Guan; Wei Wu; Hui-Shuai Zhang; Minlie Huang; Dongyan Zhao; Rui Yan

record.tranche_reason: The study develops and evaluates a dynamic module architecture, but does not test whether ablating a component causes later components to compensate for its effect.
record.gate_note: The paper cites work on attention-head functions and the Hydra effect as background, and reports results after reducing the MoM module pool. Those pool-size results do not measure downstream compensation or compare an ablated component's direct effect with its total effect.
record.test_reason: The paper proposes the Mixture-of-Modules architecture and evaluates it on validation loss, GLUE and XSUM. The Hydra effect paper appears only in the reference list; the visible text does not discuss it. The module-pool reductions are architectural choices followed by retraining, not inference-time ablations. They do not measure whether later components compensate for a removed one, and they do not compare direct with total effects. It neither tests nor uses self-repair.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. The authors conclude that MoM outperforms vanilla GPT-2 at fixed parameter count and can trade depth for efficiency. They also conclude that Transformers are over-parameterized, with attention modules more redundant than FFNs. They draw no conclusion about self-repair.
record.recipe_differences: The study proposes and evaluates a new dynamic module-assembly architecture; it does not apply the original self-repair ablation method.
record.method_sensitivity: not stated for self-repair; the study varies module-pool size and MoM configuration.

fits_no_version.finding: Shrinking the MoM-medium module pool and retraining raises validation loss little when attention modules are removed, down to NA=2. Removing FFN modules raises it more each time (Figure 3).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Attention modules in GPT-2-initialized MoM models are more redundant than FFN modules under pool reduction with retraining. This bears on redundancy, not on inference-time self-repair.

record.peer_reviewed: Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing
record.problems: The reported module-pool reduction results do not measure component-level direct effects or downstream compensation.

untested.parts: All: no attention-layer ablation, so no measure of later-layer compensation.
All: no analysis of late-MLP downregulation or erasure.
All: no per-prompt compensation distribution or overcorrection.
All: no backup heads, copy suppression, LayerNorm rescaling or anti-erasure neurons.
All: no comparison of ablation types.
All: no analysis of ablation-based attribution.

record.verdict_notes: The Hydra effect paper is listed in the references only; it is not invoked in the visible body. The record's gate note says Hydra-effect work is cited as background, which overstates its role slightly. Figure 3 also reports the other (NA, NF) loss increases, but none of them bears on self-repair.

versions.untested_parts: Layer ablation and later-layer compensation restoring the output.
Late-MLP downregulation and how it changes when earlier components are ablated.
Head ablations and compensation on the full output distribution across text, model families, and sizes.
Prompt-level variation, average compensation, and overcorrection.
The roles of backup heads, copy-suppression heads, final LayerNorm rescaling, or anti-erasure neurons in self-repair.
Self-repair under mean or resample ablations versus zero ablation.
Whether ablation-based importance scores misstate component function because of self-repair.

rows.check: Measures the validation-loss change after shrinking the module pool (NA=2, NF=3) and retraining. This is an architecture-redundancy result, not a measure of self-repair. The 0.065 value matches Figure 3 at NA=2, NF=3.
